Que.q: Q1 : What is Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright is an open-source end-to-end automation framework developed by Microsoft for testing modern web applications. It supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browsers through a single API. Playwright provides reliable automation with features like auto-waiting, network interception, screenshots, video recording, and tracing. It is widely used by QA engineers and developers to create fast and stable automated tests. Its direct browser communication makes execution faster and more reliable compared to traditional browser automation tools.

Que.note: Playwright was developed by Microsoft and supports modern web applications.

Que.q: Q2 : Which browsers are supported by Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright supports three major browser engines: Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Chromium is used for Chrome and Edge testing, Firefox supports Mozilla Firefox testing, and WebKit enables Safari testing. With a single test script, Playwright can execute tests across all supported browsers. It also provides mobile browser emulation, allowing teams to validate applications on different browser environments without maintaining separate automation frameworks.

Que.q: Q3 : Why is Playwright popular in automation testing?
Que.a: Playwright is popular because it provides fast execution, reliable automation, and powerful built-in features. It includes auto-waiting, parallel execution, screenshots, videos, tracing, API testing, and network mocking without requiring additional libraries. These capabilities reduce flaky tests and simplify framework maintenance. Playwright also supports modern web technologies such as Shadow DOM and Single Page Applications, making it a preferred automation framework for contemporary web development projects.

Que.q: Q4 : Which programming languages are supported in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and C#. This flexibility allows teams to use Playwright with their preferred programming language while maintaining the same automation capabilities. TypeScript is commonly used because of its strong type checking, while Java and C# are popular in enterprise environments. Microsoft officially maintains all supported language bindings to ensure consistency and feature parity across platforms.

Que.q: Q5 : What is the difference between Selenium and Playwright?
Que.a: Selenium communicates with browsers through the WebDriver protocol, while Playwright directly communicates with browser engines. Playwright offers built-in auto-waiting, tracing, network interception, screenshots, and API testing. Selenium often requires additional libraries for similar capabilities. Playwright generally provides faster execution and better handling of modern web applications. However, Selenium has a larger ecosystem, broader community support, and is widely used in enterprise automation projects.

Que.q: Q6 : What is auto-waiting in Playwright?
Que.a: Auto-waiting is a built-in Playwright feature that automatically waits for elements to become visible, enabled, stable, and ready before performing actions. This eliminates the need for most manual waits and sleep statements. Playwright checks whether an element is attached to the DOM, visible, and actionable before interacting with it. Auto-waiting significantly reduces flaky tests and makes automation scripts cleaner, more reliable, and easier to maintain compared to traditional automation approaches.

Que.note: Auto-waiting is one of the biggest reasons Playwright tests are less flaky.

Que.q: Q7 : How do you install Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright can be installed using Node.js and npm. After creating a project, install Playwright using npm install -D @playwright/test and then download browser binaries using npx playwright install. Playwright also provides an initialization wizard that creates configuration files and sample tests automatically. Once installation is complete, tests can be executed using the Playwright test runner. The setup process is simple and supports multiple programming languages including JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, Python, and C#.

Que.code:
npm init playwright@latest
npm install -D @playwright/test
npx playwright install

Que.q: Q8 : What is a Browser Context in Playwright?
Que.a: A Browser Context is an isolated browser session that behaves like a separate incognito window. Each context has its own cookies, cache, local storage, and session data. Multiple contexts can run within the same browser instance without sharing information. Browser Contexts are useful for testing multiple users simultaneously and improving execution speed. They form the foundation for authentication state management and parallel execution in Playwright automation frameworks.

Que.code:
const context = await browser.newContext();
const page = await context.newPage();

Que.q: Q9 : What is a Page object in Playwright?
Que.a: A Page object represents a browser tab or webpage in Playwright. It is the primary interface used to interact with web applications. Through the Page object, testers can navigate to URLs, click elements, enter text, take screenshots, handle dialogs, and validate content. Every browser context can contain multiple pages. Most Playwright automation scripts heavily rely on the Page object because it provides access to all user interactions and browser events.

Que.note: The Page object is one of the most frequently used objects in Playwright.

Que.q: Q10 : What are locators in Playwright?
Que.a: Locators are Playwright objects used to identify and interact with web elements. They are designed to be reliable and automatically support waiting and retry mechanisms. Playwright offers several locator strategies such as getByRole, getByText, getByLabel, getByPlaceholder, CSS selectors, XPath, and getByTestId. User-facing locators are recommended because they closely match how real users interact with applications and are more resistant to UI changes.

Que.q: Q11 : Which locator is mostly recommended in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright recommends using user-facing locators because they are stable, readable, and closely represent how users interact with applications. The most preferred locator is getByRole() because it uses ARIA roles and accessible names to identify elements. Other recommended locators include getByText(), getByLabel(), getByPlaceholder(), and getByTestId(). These locators reduce dependency on implementation details such as CSS classes and IDs, making tests more reliable and easier to maintain.

Que.note: getByRole() is considered the most reliable locator in Playwright.

Que.q: Q12 : What is getByRole in Playwright?
Que.a: getByRole() is a Playwright locator strategy that identifies elements based on their ARIA role and accessible name. It closely matches how assistive technologies interact with web applications, making tests more stable and accessible. Common roles include button, textbox, checkbox, link, and heading. Since getByRole focuses on user-visible behavior rather than implementation details, it is considered one of the most reliable locator strategies available in Playwright.

Que.q: Q13 : How do you launch a browser in Playwright?
Que.a: Browsers in Playwright are launched using browserType.launch() methods. Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browsers. Browsers can be launched in headless or headed mode depending on testing requirements. Additional options such as slowMo, viewport settings, and browser arguments can also be configured during launch. In Playwright Test Runner projects, browser lifecycle management is usually handled automatically through the configuration file.

Que.code: const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });

Que.note: Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit using the same API.

Que.q: Q14 : What is headless mode in Playwright?
Que.a: Headless mode allows the browser to run in the background without displaying a graphical user interface. The browser still performs all actions, executes JavaScript, and renders pages, but no browser window is visible. Headless execution is faster and consumes fewer resources, making it ideal for CI/CD pipelines and automated test environments. Playwright uses headless mode by default, although it can be disabled when visual debugging is required.

Que.q: Q15 : What is headed mode in Playwright?
Que.a: Headed mode runs the browser with a visible graphical interface so testers can observe every action during execution. It is commonly used while developing, debugging, and troubleshooting automation scripts. Testers can visually verify browser interactions such as clicks, form submissions, and navigation steps. Headed mode can be enabled through browser launch options or command-line flags. Although slower than headless execution, it provides excellent visibility into test behavior.

Que.code: const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });

Que.note: Headed mode is extremely useful when debugging failed automation tests.

Que.q: Q16 : How do you take screenshots in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright provides a built-in screenshot() method to capture screenshots during test execution. Screenshots can be taken for the entire page, visible viewport, or a specific element. They are commonly used for debugging failures, visual verification, and reporting. Playwright also supports automatic screenshot capture on test failures through configuration settings. Screenshots help testers quickly identify UI issues and understand the application state when a test fails.

Que.note: Playwright can automatically capture screenshots for failed test cases.

Que.q: Q17 : What is Trace Viewer in Playwright?
Que.a: Trace Viewer is a powerful debugging tool that records every step of a Playwright test execution. It captures screenshots, DOM snapshots, network activity, console logs, and user actions. The generated trace file can be opened later to visually replay the test and investigate failures. Trace Viewer is especially useful in CI/CD environments where testers cannot directly observe browser execution. It provides detailed insights into what happened before, during, and after a test failure.

Que.q: Q18 : What is Playwright Inspector?
Que.a: Playwright Inspector is an interactive debugging tool that helps developers and testers inspect locators, pause execution, step through test actions, and analyze application behavior. It opens alongside the browser and highlights the currently executing test step. Inspector also suggests recommended locators and allows interactive test debugging. This tool is extremely useful while developing automation scripts because it simplifies locator identification and troubleshooting of failed test cases.

Que.note: Inspector can generate recommended Playwright locators automatically.

Que.q: Q19 : How do you handle dropdowns in Playwright?
Que.a: Dropdowns in Playwright are handled using the selectOption() method for standard HTML select elements. Options can be selected using visible text, value attributes, or indexes. For custom dropdowns built with div elements, regular click actions are used to open the dropdown and select an option. Playwright also supports multiple selections in multi-select dropdowns. After selecting an option, validations should be performed to ensure the correct value has been chosen.

Que.q: Q20 : How do you handle alerts in Playwright?
Que.a: Alerts, confirmation dialogs, and prompt dialogs are handled using the dialog event in Playwright. Testers can accept, dismiss, or provide input to dialogs through dialog methods. Event handlers should be registered before performing the action that triggers the dialog. Playwright automatically dismisses dialogs if no handler is provided, preventing tests from hanging. Dialog handling is commonly used when validating delete confirmations, alerts, and prompt-based user interactions.

Que.q: Q21 : How do you handle frames in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright handles frames using frameLocator() and frame() methods. The recommended approach is frameLocator() because it integrates with Playwright locators and supports auto-waiting. Unlike Selenium, Playwright does not require switching in and out of frames, making automation simpler and cleaner. Frames are commonly used for embedded content such as payment gateways, advertisements, and external widgets. Playwright can easily interact with elements inside single or nested iframes using dedicated frame locators.

Que.code:
const frame = page.frameLocator('#iframeId');
await frame.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();

Que.note: frameLocator() is the preferred method for handling iframes in Playwright.

Que.q: Q22 : How do you handle multiple tabs in Playwright?
Que.a: Multiple tabs are handled using browser contexts and page events. When a user action opens a new tab, Playwright captures it through the page event. The new tab is represented by a separate Page object, allowing independent interactions. Testers can switch between tabs by referencing different page variables. This approach makes handling multiple browser tabs straightforward and reliable, especially when validating external links, product pages, or third-party integrations.

Que.note: Every browser tab is represented by a separate Page object.

Que.q: Q23 : What is Page Object Model in Playwright?
Que.a: Page Object Model (POM) is a design pattern that separates page elements and business actions from test scripts. Each page is represented by a dedicated class containing locators and reusable methods. This improves code maintainability, readability, and reusability. When UI changes occur, updates are required only in the page class instead of multiple test files. POM is widely used in Playwright frameworks to build scalable and maintainable automation solutions.

Que.q: Q24 : What is the use of beforeEach in Playwright?
Que.a: beforeEach is a Playwright hook that runs before every test case. It is typically used for common setup activities such as launching applications, logging in users, creating test data, or navigating to a specific page. By placing repetitive setup logic in beforeEach, test scripts become shorter and easier to maintain. It also ensures every test starts from a consistent state, improving reliability and reducing dependencies between test cases.

Que.note: beforeEach executes before every individual test case.

Que.q: Q25 : What is the use of afterEach in Playwright?
Que.a: afterEach is a Playwright hook that executes after every test case, regardless of whether the test passes or fails. It is mainly used for cleanup activities such as logging out users, deleting test data, capturing logs, taking screenshots, or closing resources. Proper cleanup ensures test isolation and prevents one test from affecting another. Using afterEach helps maintain a stable and predictable test environment throughout execution.

Que.note: afterEach runs even when a test case fails.

Que.q: Q26 : What is parallel execution in Playwright?
Que.a: Parallel execution allows multiple test cases or test files to run simultaneously, reducing overall execution time. Playwright supports parallel execution through worker processes that run tests independently. Each worker uses isolated browser contexts to prevent data sharing between tests. This approach improves efficiency, especially for large regression suites. Parallel execution is commonly configured in playwright.config.js and is widely used in CI/CD pipelines to speed up automated testing and provide faster feedback.

Que.note: Tests should be independent when using parallel execution.

Que.q: Q27 : What is Playwright Test Runner?
Que.a: Playwright Test Runner is the official testing framework provided by Playwright. It offers features such as test execution, assertions, hooks, retries, parallel execution, reporting, fixtures, and browser management. The Test Runner automatically handles browser setup and cleanup, allowing testers to focus on writing test logic. It integrates seamlessly with Playwright features and supports modern testing practices, making it the recommended choice for Playwright automation projects.

Que.note: @playwright/test is the official Playwright Test Runner package.

Que.q: Q28 : What are assertions in Playwright?
Que.a: Assertions are validations that compare actual application behavior with expected results. Playwright provides web-first assertions through the expect API, which automatically wait for conditions before failing. Common assertions verify visibility, text, URL, title, checkbox state, and element presence. Assertions improve test reliability by reducing timing issues and ensuring application functionality behaves correctly. They are a fundamental part of automated testing and help determine whether a test passes or fails.

Que.q: Q29 : How do you wait for an element in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright automatically waits for most element interactions, but explicit waiting can be used when necessary. Testers commonly use web-first assertions such as expect(locator).toBeVisible() or methods like waitForSelector(), waitForURL(), and waitForLoadState(). These approaches wait for specific conditions before continuing execution. Using meaningful waits instead of fixed delays improves test stability, reduces flakiness, and ensures faster execution by waiting only when required.

Que.note: Prefer assertions over hardcoded waits like setTimeout or sleep.

Que.q: Q30 : How do you upload files in Playwright?
Que.a: File uploads in Playwright are handled using the setInputFiles() method. This method directly assigns files to file input elements without interacting with operating system dialogs. Playwright supports uploading single files, multiple files, and clearing uploaded files when required. The approach is simple, reliable, and works consistently across browsers. File upload functionality is commonly tested in document management systems, profile image uploads, and form submission workflows.

Que.q: Q31 : How do you download files in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright handles file downloads through the download event. When a download is triggered, Playwright captures it and provides a Download object that can be used to save and verify the file. The recommended approach is to wait for the download event before performing the action that starts the download. This ensures reliable file handling and allows testers to validate downloaded files as part of automated test scenarios.

Que.note: Playwright does not require special browser settings for handling downloads.

Que.q: Q32 : What is API testing in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright provides built-in API testing capabilities through APIRequestContext. Testers can send HTTP requests such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE directly without opening a browser. API testing is useful for validating backend services, preparing test data, and verifying application behavior. Combining UI and API testing in a single framework improves efficiency, reduces execution time, and allows more comprehensive end-to-end validation.

Que.q: Q33 : What is the use of fixtures in Playwright?
Que.a: Fixtures in Playwright provide reusable setup and teardown functionality through dependency injection. Built-in fixtures include browser, context, page, and request. Custom fixtures can also be created to manage authenticated sessions, page objects, or test data. Fixtures help reduce duplicate code, improve maintainability, and ensure a consistent test environment. They are widely used in large automation frameworks to simplify test creation and resource management.

Que.note: Fixtures automatically manage setup and cleanup of resources.

Que.q: Q34 : What is test.describe in Playwright?
Que.a: test.describe is used to group related test cases into logical sections. It helps organize test files and improves readability by keeping feature-specific tests together. Each describe block can have its own hooks such as beforeEach and afterEach. Grouping tests also makes reports easier to understand and supports configuration options like parallel execution within a specific group. It is considered a best practice when creating structured automation frameworks.

Que.note: test.describe improves organization and readability of test suites.

Que.q: Q35 : What is test.only in Playwright?
Que.a: test.only is a Playwright modifier used to execute only a specific test or group of tests while skipping all others. It is useful during development and debugging when focusing on a particular test case. Using test.only speeds up troubleshooting because only the selected test runs. However, developers should remove test.only before committing code because it can unintentionally skip important tests in automated pipelines.

Que.note: Never commit test.only to source control as it skips all other tests.

Que.q: Q36 : What is test.skip in Playwright?
Que.a: test.skip is a Playwright modifier used to skip test execution intentionally. Skipped tests appear in reports but are not executed. It is useful when a feature is under development, a known bug exists, or a test is not applicable for certain environments or browsers. Playwright also supports conditional skipping based on runtime conditions. Using test.skip helps teams manage unstable or temporary scenarios without removing test cases from the automation suite.

Que.note: Skipped tests are shown in reports but are not executed.

Que.q: Q37 : What is the use of hooks in Playwright?
Que.a: Hooks are lifecycle methods that execute before or after tests. Playwright provides beforeAll, beforeEach, afterEach, and afterAll hooks. They are used for setup and cleanup activities such as launching applications, creating test data, logging in users, deleting test records, and releasing resources. Hooks improve code reusability and keep test cases focused on business logic. They also ensure consistency by preparing a predictable environment for every test execution.

Que.q: Q38 : How do you generate reports in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright provides built-in reporting capabilities including HTML, List, Dot, JSON, and JUnit reporters. The HTML report is the most commonly used because it provides detailed information about passed, failed, and skipped tests along with screenshots, videos, and traces. Reports help teams analyze execution results and troubleshoot failures. Reporter configurations are defined in playwright.config.js and can be integrated with CI/CD tools for automated reporting.

Que.note: Use 'npx playwright show-report' to open the generated HTML report.

Que.q: Q39 : What is retry functionality in Playwright?
Que.a: Retry functionality automatically reruns failed tests a specified number of times before marking them as failed. It helps reduce false failures caused by temporary issues such as network delays or unstable environments. Retries are configured in playwright.config.js and are commonly enabled in CI/CD pipelines. Although retries improve execution stability, consistently failing tests should be investigated instead of relying on retries as a permanent solution.

Que.note: Retries help identify flaky tests but should not replace proper debugging.

Que.q: Q40 : What is the difference between fill() and type() in Playwright?
Que.a: fill() and type() are both used to enter text into input fields, but they behave differently. fill() clears existing content and instantly sets the entire value, making it faster and more reliable. type() simulates real keyboard typing by sending characters one at a time and triggering keyboard events. fill() is preferred for most automation scenarios, while type() is useful when applications rely on keypress events, autocomplete behavior, or input masking functionality.

Que.q: Q41 : How do you perform mouse actions in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright provides several methods for performing mouse actions such as click, double-click, right-click, hover, and drag-and-drop. High-level locator methods are recommended because they automatically handle waiting and retries. For advanced interactions, the mouse API can move the cursor to specific coordinates and simulate mouse button actions. Mouse operations are useful for testing menus, tooltips, drag-and-drop functionality, and other interactive web application features.

Que.q: Q42 : How do you handle keyboard actions in Playwright?
Que.a: Keyboard actions in Playwright can be performed using locator.press() or the keyboard API. Playwright supports typing text, pressing special keys, keyboard shortcuts, and key combinations. Common actions include Enter, Tab, Escape, Arrow keys, and Control-based shortcuts. Keyboard automation is useful for testing accessibility, form navigation, search functionality, and applications that rely heavily on keyboard interactions. Playwright accurately simulates real user keyboard behavior.

Que.q: Q43 : What is network interception in Playwright?
Que.a: Network interception allows Playwright to monitor, modify, block, or mock network requests and responses during test execution. Using page.route(), testers can simulate successful responses, server errors, slow networks, or unavailable services. This helps validate application behavior under different conditions without depending on real backend systems. Network interception is particularly useful for testing error handling, API integrations, and edge cases that are difficult to reproduce consistently.

Que.note: Network interception helps test application behavior without relying on actual backend services.

Que.q: Q44 : How do you run Playwright tests from the command line?
Que.a: Playwright tests are executed using the Playwright Test Runner command-line interface. Testers can run all tests, specific test files, browser-specific tests, debug sessions, and parallel executions through different command options. Command-line execution is widely used in local development and CI/CD pipelines. Playwright also supports filtering tests, generating reports, and controlling execution behavior through command flags, making automation management flexible and efficient.

Que.q: Q45 : What is CI/CD integration in Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright integrates easily with CI/CD platforms such as GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, and GitLab CI. Automated test execution can be triggered whenever code changes are committed, ensuring continuous quality validation. Playwright runs efficiently in headless mode and supports parallel execution, reporting, screenshots, traces, and videos. CI/CD integration helps teams detect issues early, reduce manual effort, and maintain software quality throughout the development lifecycle.

Que.note: Playwright is commonly executed in headless mode within CI/CD pipelines.

Que.q: Q46 : What are the advantages of Playwright?
Que.a: Playwright offers several advantages including fast execution, cross-browser support, auto-waiting, parallel execution, API testing, network interception, and built-in debugging tools. It reduces flaky tests by automatically waiting for elements to become ready before interaction. Playwright also supports screenshots, videos, traces, and mobile emulation without requiring additional libraries. These features simplify automation framework development and make Playwright a powerful solution for testing modern web applications efficiently.

Que.note: Playwright provides many features out of the box that require additional tools in other frameworks.

Que.q: Q47 : What are the limitations of Playwright?
Que.a: Although Playwright is powerful, it has some limitations. It is primarily focused on web application automation and does not support desktop application testing. The community ecosystem is smaller than Selenium's, and some organizations still have large Selenium-based frameworks that are costly to migrate. Learning advanced Playwright concepts such as fixtures, tracing, and network interception may require additional effort. However, Playwright continues to evolve rapidly and gain industry adoption.

Que.note: Despite limitations, Playwright is one of the fastest-growing automation frameworks.

Que.q: Q48 : Why is Playwright preferred for modern web applications?
Que.a: Playwright is preferred for modern web applications because it handles dynamic content, asynchronous operations, and single-page applications effectively. Features such as auto-waiting, web-first assertions, network interception, and browser context isolation improve test reliability. It also supports Shadow DOM, multiple tabs, API testing, and mobile emulation. These capabilities make Playwright well-suited for modern frontend technologies such as React, Angular, and Vue applications where traditional automation tools may face challenges.

Que.note: Playwright was designed specifically to address challenges faced in modern web automation.

Que.q: Q49 : What is authentication state in Playwright?
Que.a: Authentication state is a Playwright feature that allows testers to save and reuse logged-in session information across multiple test executions. Instead of performing login steps before every test, Playwright stores cookies and local storage data in a state file. Tests can then load this file to start in an authenticated state. This reduces execution time, improves efficiency, and simplifies framework design for applications requiring user authentication.

Que.note: Authentication state is commonly used in Playwright framework setup projects.

Que.q: Q50 : Why should companies choose Playwright?
Que.a: Companies choose Playwright because it offers modern automation capabilities, fast execution, excellent browser support, and built-in testing utilities. Features such as auto-waiting, tracing, screenshots, videos, network mocking, and API testing reduce framework complexity and maintenance effort. Playwright integrates smoothly with CI/CD pipelines and cloud platforms, helping teams deliver high-quality software faster. Its reliability and support for modern web technologies make it a strong choice for contemporary automation projects.

Que.note: Many organizations are adopting Playwright for new automation projects because of its modern architecture.
